content_voiceover: This slide covers phenotype-matched, or extended phenotype-matched, red cell release, used for AIHA patients and also for patients on daratumumab. The purpose is simple, reduce red cell alloimmunization, meaning prevent the patient from forming new red cell antibodies against minor blood group antigens. Three scenarios call for this strategy. First, chronically transfused patients, like those with thalassemia or sickle cell disease, who receive so many units over a lifetime that their alloimmunization risk climbs steeply without matching. Second, patients with autoimmune hemolytic disease, where ongoing antibody activity and frequent transfusion needs make new alloantibody formation especially likely and especially hard to detect against a background of autoantibody. Third, and this is a high-yield, testable point, patients on CD38 or CD47 antibody drugs, such as daratumumab, because these therapeutic antibodies bind red cells and cause pan-reactive agglutination that mimics or masks alloantibodies on the antibody screen, so extended phenotype or genotype matching becomes essential before treatment even starts.
keypoints: Goal of phenotype-matched RBC transfusion is to prevent red cell alloimmunization
Chronically transfused patients (thalassemia, sickle cell disease) need extended matching due to cumulative exposure
Autoimmune hemolytic disease patients benefit, since it reduces confounding alloantibody formation
CD38/CD47 drugs like daratumumab cause pan-reactive interference; match phenotype or genotype before therapy starts
keypoint_voiceover: Key exam point, phenotype-matched RBC transfusion aims to prevent alloimmunization. It's used in three settings, chronically transfused patients like thalassemia or sickle cell disease, patients with autoimmune hemolytic disease, and patients starting CD38 or CD47 antibody drugs like daratumumab, which cause pan-agglutination on testing. For daratumumab patients especially, get baseline extended typing before therapy begins.
